primitives.name: Incremental Tracklet Classification
primitives.verbatim_quote: Then an incremental learning mechanism trains a Transformer to classify identities using few game-specific human annotations.
primitives.assumptions: Tracklets are temporally coherent; player identities remain consistent within game context.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When annotation frequency drops below 6 tracklets per player, classification accuracy degrades.

layer2.mapping: The Transformer learns to associate feature embeddings (F) with player identities (I) through supervised fine-tuning on labeled tracklets (L), enabling generalization to unseen game segments.

primitives.name: Semi-Supervised Detection and Reidentification
primitives.verbatim_quote: Non-ambiguous tracklets and their appearance features are automatically generated with a detection and a reidentification network both pre-trained on public datasets.
primitives.assumptions: Pre-trained networks generalize to team sport contexts; visual similarity correlates with identity.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Performance degrades under significant occlusion or uniform jersey wear.

layer2.mapping: Detection (D) and ReID (R) networks jointly produce bounding boxes (B) and embeddings (E) that form a canonical representation of player identity in video space.
layer2.telemetry: IoU between predicted and ground truth bounding boxes.

primitives.name: Minimal Annotation Tracking
primitives.verbatim_quote: We also show that our method is able to track rugby sevens players during a full match, if they are observable at a minimal resolution, with the annotation of only 6 few seconds length tracklets per player.
primitives.assumptions: Each annotated tracklet captures sufficient discriminative features; minimal annotations suffice for full match coverage.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Tracking fails when resolution falls below R or annotation count exceeds 6 per player.

layer2.mapping: The system maps minimal annotation input (A) into full match coverage (M) via learned identity associations, assuming sufficient visual distinctiveness at low resolution.
layer2.telemetry: Percentage of match successfully tracked with <6 tracklets per player.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that traditional multi-object tracking (MOT) methods fail in team sports due to high-speed movement, frequent occlusion, and identical uniform wear. The proposed solution leverages semi-supervised detection and reidentification using pre-trained networks to extract appearance features from bounding boxes. These features are then used in a Transformer-based classifier trained incrementally with minimal human annotations—specifically, 6-second tracklets per player. This approach enables scalable tracking without requiring extensive manual labeling. The key mathematical duality lies in the separation of feature extraction (via D and R) and identity classification (via T), where T learns from L to generalize to I. Failure modes include insufficient annotation, poor resolution, or misalignment between appearance and identity. The system's robustness stems from its ability to operate under uncertainty while maintaining probabilistic consistency through Bayesian inference.
